chapters.title: A Wall Longer Than the Great Wall of China

pages.text: Most people have heard of the Great Wall of China. Fewer people have heard of the Great Wall of Benin. This is surprising, because the Great Wall of Benin was, by some measurements, the largest earthwork ever built in human history, longer and more extensive than the Great Wall of China itself.

image.note: Map of Nigeria showing Benin City and the surrounding network of earthworks

pages.text: The Great Wall of Benin is not a single wall. It is a vast network of ditches and ramparts, earthen banks reinforced with clay, that once enclosed the city of Benin and the farmland and villages surrounding it. The total length of all the ditches and banks in the network has been estimated at more than 16,000 kilometres. That is longer than the distance from Lagos to London and back again.

The network was built by the Edo people of the Benin Kingdom, one of the most powerful and sophisticated civilisations in West African history. Construction began as far back as the ninth or tenth century CE and continued for hundreds of years, expanding as the kingdom grew. At its greatest extent, the Benin Kingdom controlled a large area of what is now southern Nigeria.

The walls were not purely defensive, though they served that purpose too. They were also a statement of power, a declaration to anyone approaching Benin City that this was a place of authority, wealth, and organisation. Only a civilisation with the resources, the knowledge, and the collective will to sustain a centuries-long building project could have created them.

image.note: Diagram showing cross-section of a typical rampart and ditch with approximate measurements

pages.text: To understand the scale of the walls, imagine standing at the bottom of one of the great ditches. The bank rises above you like a two-storey building. In places, the combined height from the ditch floor to the top of the rampart was more than fifteen metres. An enemy would have to climb down one side and up the other, in full view of defenders, before reaching the city. Most did not try.

The walls also organised daily life. Gates controlled who entered and left, and tolls could be collected from traders passing through. Inside the enclosures, families farmed, kept markets, and settled disputes under the authority of the Oba's officials. The earthworks were not only a fortress. They were a map of the kingdom's power, drawn on the land itself, showing every visitor exactly where Benin's authority began.

The Benin Kingdom was ruled by the Oba, a king regarded as both a political and a spiritual authority. The Obas of Benin were among the most powerful rulers in West Africa. Their court was renowned for its art, its ceremony, and the strict protocol that governed every aspect of life in Benin City.

The Benin Kingdom is perhaps best known today for its bronzes: plaques, sculptures, and heads cast in brass and bronze that decorated the royal palace and were used in royal ceremonies. These works are among the finest examples of metalwork produced anywhere in the ancient world. Their technique is extraordinary: the lost-wax casting method used by Benin artists produces objects of remarkable detail and precision.

image.note: Illustration of a Benin bronze head with annotations describing the casting technique

pages.text: In 1897, a British military expedition attacked and burned Benin City, killing many people and destroying much of the royal palace. British soldiers seized thousands of bronze artworks and took them to Britain. These objects, known as the Benin Bronzes, ended up in museums across Europe and North America. The question of where they belong, and whether they should be returned to Nigeria, is one of the most debated cultural questions of our time.

The Oba of Benin continues to this day. The current Oba is Ewuare II, who ascended the throne in 2016. The royal palace in Benin City has been rebuilt. The Benin Kingdom's traditions of governance, art, and ceremony have been maintained across centuries of enormous change.

The lost-wax casting method worked like this. First, the artist sculpted the object in beeswax, capturing every fine detail. The wax model was then coated in layers of clay and left to dry into a hard mould. When the mould was heated, the wax melted and ran out, leaving a perfect hollow space. Molten brass was poured in. Once cooled, the clay was broken away, revealing the metal sculpture inside. Each mould could be used only once, so every Benin bronze is unique.

The casters belonged to a hereditary guild, and their skills passed from father to son over centuries. They lived and worked in a district of Benin City that still exists today: Igun Street, now recognised by UNESCO. Modern visitors to Benin City can watch descendants of the royal casters working with techniques their ancestors perfected hundreds of years ago. The guild survived the destruction of 1897. The knowledge did not die.

In recent years, museums in Europe and North America have begun returning Benin Bronzes to Nigeria. Germany has returned more than a thousand objects. Universities and museums in Britain and the United States have followed with returns of their own. A new museum is planned in Benin City to house the returned works. The story of the bronzes, which began with creation and continued through theft, is now entering a third chapter: homecoming.

The construction of the Great Wall of Benin was not a single project with a start and an end. It grew over many centuries, as the kingdom expanded and the need to enclose new areas arose. Each new section was planned, excavated, and built by communities under the direction of the Oba's court.

The method was earthwork: the builders dug a wide, deep ditch, and the earth removed from the ditch was piled alongside it to form a raised bank or rampart. The rampart was then reinforced with clay, compacted and shaped. In some places, the ditches were several metres deep and the ramparts several metres high. Together, ditch and rampart presented a formidable obstacle to anyone approaching without permission.

The labour involved was enormous. Estimates suggest that the total volume of earth moved to create the Great Wall of Benin was more than one hundred times the volume of material in the Great Pyramid of Giza. This calculation alone gives some sense of the scale of the achievement. The people of the Benin Kingdom moved more earth than almost any other civilisation in the ancient world.

image.note: Comparative diagram: volume of earth moved for Benin walls versus Great Pyramid of Giza

pages.text: Unlike stone construction, earthworks require constant maintenance. Rain erodes ditches and softens banks. Without regular attention, the walls would gradually return to flat ground. That the Great Wall of Benin existed for hundreds of years as a functioning system of fortifications and boundaries is evidence of sustained, organised effort across many generations.

Archaeologists studying the earthworks face an unusual problem: the walls are so long that simply mapping them is a career's work. The pioneering researcher Patrick Darling spent decades walking, measuring, and recording thousands of kilometres of banks and ditches, often through thick bush. Much of what the world knows about the scale of the network comes from his surveys. Even so, large sections have never been properly mapped. The full extent may never be known.

Dating the earthworks is equally difficult. Earth banks do not carry inscriptions. Researchers rely on fragments of pottery buried in the walls, on charcoal that can be scientifically dated, and on the oral histories of the communities who live along the network. These methods suggest construction across many centuries, with different sections built at different times. The Great Wall of Benin was not one project. It was hundreds of projects, joined across generations into a single vast idea.

The Great Wall of Benin today is a shadow of what it once was. Much of the network was destroyed in the twentieth century as Benin City expanded, and land that had once been protected earthwork was built over, farmed, or simply left to erode. What remains is a fraction of the original system.

However, significant sections of the earthworks survive, particularly in the rural areas outside Benin City. These sections are now recognised as an archaeological site of global importance. Researchers from Nigerian universities and international institutions are working to map, study, and protect what remains.

There is growing recognition, both in Nigeria and internationally, that the Great Wall of Benin deserves a place among the world's great heritage sites. Campaigns to have the surviving sections listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site are ongoing. The argument is simple: this is one of the greatest feats of construction in human history, and it was built in Africa, by Africans, without any European involvement or knowledge.

Nigeria is not the only place where ancient communities built monumental earthworks. A separate but equally remarkable system exists at Sungbo's Eredo in Ogun State, south-west Nigeria. This network of ditches and ramparts was built by the Ijebu people and is associated in local tradition with a powerful woman named Orimiri Iyasere Sungbo. It is distinct from the Benin Kingdom walls in both location and origin: different people, different century, different purpose. That two Nigerian peoples, entirely independently, chose to build their power and identity into the earth on such a scale is itself extraordinary. The full history of both systems is still being uncovered.

What can a young Nigerian do with this history? First, know it. The walls of Benin are barely taught, barely marked, and barely protected, yet they are among the greatest constructions in human history. Second, visit. Sections of the earthworks and the royal palace can be seen in and around Benin City. Third, tell the story. Monuments survive when people care about them. The pyramids of Egypt are famous because Egyptians made the world pay attention. Benin deserves the same.
